verses.text: How the city sits solitary, that was full of people! She has become as a widow, who was great among the nations! She who was a princess among the provinces has become tributary!
She weeps bitterly in the night, and her tears are on her cheeks; among all her lovers she has no one to comfort her: All her friends have dealt treacherously with her; they have become her enemies.
Judah has gone into captivity because of affliction, and because of great servitude; she dwells among the nations, she finds no rest: all her persecutors overtook her within the straits.
The ways of Zion mourn, because no one come to the solemn assembly; all her gates are desolate, her priests sigh: her virgins are afflicted, and she herself is in bitterness.
Her adversaries have become the head, her enemies prosper; for Yahweh  has afflicted her for the multitude of her transgressions: her young children have gone into captivity before the adversary.
All majesty has departed from the daughter of Zion: her princes have become like deer that find no pasture, they have gone without strength before the pursuer.

Jerusalem remembers in the days of her affliction and of her miseries all her pleasant things that were from the days of old: when her people fell into the hand of the adversary, and no one helped her, The adversaries saw her, they mocked at her desolations.
Jerusalem has grievously sinned; therefore she has become as an unclean thing; all who honored her despise her, because they have seen her nakedness: yes, she sighs, and turns backward.

Her filthiness was in her skirts; she didn’t remember her latter end; therefore she has come down astoundingly; she has no comforter: “See, Yahweh, my affliction; for the enemy has magnified himself.”

The adversary has spread out his hand on all her pleasant things: for she has seen that the nations are entered into her sanctuary, concerning whom you commanded that they should not enter into your assembly.
All her people sigh, they seek bread; they have given their pleasant things for food to refresh the soul: “Look, Yahweh, and see; for I have become abject.”
“Is it nothing to you, all you who pass by? Look, and see if there is any sorrow like my sorrow, which is brought on me, with which Yahweh has afflicted me in the day of his fierce anger.
“From on high has he sent fire into my bones, and it prevails against them; He has spread a net for my feet. He has turned me back. He has made me desolate and faint all day long.

“The yoke of my transgressions is bound by his hand; They are knit together. They have come up on my neck. He has made my strength to fail. The Lord  has delivered me into their hands, against whom I am not able to stand.
“The Lord has set at nothing all my mighty men within me. He has called a solemn assembly against me to crush my young men. The Lord has trodden as in a wine press the virgin daughter of Judah.
“For these things I weep. My eye, my eye runs down with water, because the comforter who should refresh my soul is far from me. My children are desolate, because the enemy has prevailed.”

Zion spreads out her hands. There is no one to comfort her; Yahweh has commanded concerning Jacob, that those who are around him should be his adversaries. Jerusalem is among them as an unclean thing.
“Yahweh is righteous; for I have rebelled against his commandment. Please hear all you peoples, and see my sorrow. My virgins and my young men have gone into captivity.
“I called for my lovers, but they deceived me. My priests and my elders gave up the spirit in the city, while they sought food for themselves to refresh their souls.
“See, Yahweh; for I am in distress. My heart is troubled. My heart is turned within me, for I have grievously rebelled. Abroad the sword bereaves. At home it is like death.

“They have heard that I sigh. There is no one to comfort me. All my enemies have heard of my trouble. They are glad that you have done it: You will bring the day that you have proclaimed, and they will be like me.
“Let all their wickedness come before you; Do to them as you have done to me for all my transgressions. For my sighs are many, and my heart is faint.

footnotes.content: Jerusalem sits alone—once crowded with life, now widowed and stripped of her glory. Sometimes we know such silence. When the Lord allows emptying, it is never because He has forgotten us, but often to teach us that our security was never in crowds or standing, but in Him alone.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Those she called lovers and friends turn to enemies in her night of weeping. How quickly fair-weather comfort fails. In such moments, Christ's steady presence becomes the only comfort worth having—He weeps with us and does not leave.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Judah is taken into captivity—first to Assyria in 722 BC, now to Babylon in 586 BC. Her straits are literal: trapped between pursuers with nowhere to run. Yet even in chains, the faithful remnant carries the knowledge of God's covenant. He has not ceased to be God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The solemn assembly does not gather; the priests sigh instead of leading praise. When worship ceases and joy drains away, the silence itself becomes a sermon about what we have lost. Yet God can restore the singing—He alone knows how.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The writer traces the cause plainly: Yahweh has afflicted her for her transgressions. This is not bitterness speaking—it is honest acknowledgment. The Lord's judgment is righteous, and to accept it humbly is the beginning of restoration. The children in captivity bear the cost their parents chose.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Her princes, who should have led with strength, are now like starving deer—helpless and hunted. When pride falls and power fails, we learn how small we are. The Lord alone holds stable ground; all earthly glory trembles.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jerusalem remembers her former loveliness—the days of old when she was filled with people and joy. The mockery of her enemies cuts deepest because the loss is real. To grieve what we have lost honestly is faithful; we need not pretend the ruin tastes like blessing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Her sin is grievous—she has become an unclean thing to those who once honored her. The shame of exposure is itself a judgment; those we thought would stand by us now turn away. Yet Christ bore our shame on a cross, and in Him we are never finally despised.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She did not remember her latter end—did not foresee the judgment coming. Now she falls astonishingly, like a garment weighted with uncleanness, with no one to lift her. Yet her cry to Yahweh shows she has not lost faith entirely: she still calls Him to look and see her affliction.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The sanctuary is defiled by the nations. Deuteronomy 23:3 commanded that foreigners should not enter the assembly of the Lord; now they profane His holy house. The violation of sacred space adds a spiritual depth to the physical conquest—not only bodies are conquered, but the very dwelling place of God seems surrendered.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Her people trade their treasures for bread to survive. Hunger strips away all pride; when the belly is empty, the grandest things become worthless. The cry to Yahweh comes from the bone-deep need of those who have nothing left to trade but their own lowliness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She calls out to passersby: "Is there any sorrow like mine?" Her pain feels singular, unmatched. Yet in her deepest cry, she bears witness to all who have known the Lord's fierce anger for their sin. Her sorrow becomes a mirror; others see their own ruin there.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Fire sent from on high into her bones—the judge strikes from heaven, inward. Her feet are netted; she is turned backward, made faint all day. The imagery is visceral: judgment is not abstract but felt in the body. Yet even as she names it, she speaks to Yahweh, still calling on the very One who afflicts.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The yoke of transgressions is bound by His hand—not by chance or accident, but by the Lord's own judgment, knit tight and heavy on her neck. Her strength fails because she cannot bear it. To confess this truth is terrible and true; Christ alone bore a yoke we could never lift.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord treads her like a winepress, crushing the virgin daughter of Judah. The image is brutal and exact—those with the strength to defend her are made nothing; the tender are crushed beneath the weight of judgment. Yet a winepress produces wine; judgment's end is not mere destruction.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She weeps, and her eyes run with tears—there is no comforter to refresh her soul. The one who should comfort is far away. Her children are desolate because the enemy has won. Yet her tears are not silent; she calls them forth as testimony to what the Lord sees.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zion spreads out empty hands—a gesture of both prayer and surrender. The Lord has commanded that those around Jacob become his adversaries; the very people who should defend him have become his foes. She is alone among them, unclean, despised. Yet she spreads her hands still.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh is righteous—Jerusalem confesses the judge's justice. She has rebelled against His commandment, and she names it plainly. Her virgins and young men have gone into captivity; the generational loss is real and grievous. Yet to acknowledge the Lord's righteousness even in judgment is to begin the journey back to Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She called for lovers and priests—those who should have helped—and they failed her. The priests, who should have interceded, gave up; they sought food to survive rather than leading their people in repentance. The failure of leaders in crisis is a bitter lesson learned too late.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The sword kills abroad; at home, death itself lives. Enemies and famine together have consumed her land and people. Her heart turns within her as she names her own rebellion—she has grievously sinned. The inward turning is the first movement toward repentance; she begins to see herself as the Lord sees her.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Her enemies hear her sigh and are glad; they celebrate because the Lord has done it—His judgment is evident to all. Yet in this, she has spoken her own future: she calls on the Lord to bring judgment on them as He has done to her. The same sword cuts both ways.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in this closing plea: all her wickedness laid bare before the Lord, all her transgressions brought into the light. We too are called to cease hiding and to bring our sighing hearts before Him. His judgment is righteous; in Him alone is mercy for the guilty.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
